title: NEW SPEEDRUN!!! Fly to a Higher Elo | French, Nimzowitsch | Top Gun Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The knight to c6 is already off the main road — the book move here is the pawn to d5. It's a perfectly playable developing move, but it's a warning too: don't assume an offbeat setup is losing just because it isn't theory.
moves.teaches: Against a non-theoretical move, don't relax — treat it on its merits, not as a free win.
moves.plans: Develop soundly and wait for a target.

moves.spoken: No need to rush the pawn to d5 with nothing developed yet — the simplest is to get the knight to f3. Once the pieces are out, the central breaks d5 and e5 become real; premature, they're just concrete for its own sake.
moves.teaches: Finish development before committing to a concrete central break.
moves.plans: Develop first, break in the centre later.

moves.spoken: Black's pawn to d6 is another passive, unforcing choice. Play it as primitively as possible — the knight to c3, keeping it in the spirit of e4. The pawn to c4 would be reasonable, but that's really a queen's-pawn way of playing.
moves.teaches: In an e4 opening, natural piece development beats grabbing extra space with c4.

moves.spoken: The bishop to d3 is the square I want: it reinforces the e4-pawn and, once Black castles, prepares the pawn to e5 with the bishop staring at h7. The queen later joins on e4 — bishop and queen aimed at h7 is a real mate threat. Note the point: even when the h-pawn moves, the square it left behind stays weak.
moves.teaches: A moved pawn can fix nothing — the square it vacated may be the lasting weakness.
moves.plans: Bd3 then Qe4, battery on the b1-h7 diagonal.

moves.spoken: Castle and keep making the most standard moves — the knight jump to b4 isn't even a threat, since the bishop just steps back and a3 shoos it away. Black's pawn to b6 ignores the kingside, and that's what invites punishment: to punish slow development you open the centre, because open files are direct pathways to the king and to loose pieces.
moves.teaches: Punishing slow development means opening the centre — files are highways to the king and to loose pieces.
moves.plans: Castle, then break to open lines.

moves.spoken: This is the dynamite: the pawn to d5. The d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and advancing onto them forces the centre open. Two moves do the job, but only this one opens the file I actually want — the e-file, the direct path to Black's king.
moves.teaches: Advance onto the opponent's pawn hooks to force the file you want open — here, the e-file.
moves.plans: d5 to rip open the e-file.

moves.spoken: Recapturing on d5 completes the operation — the e-file is open straight at Black's uncastled king, and this is exactly why castling early mattered: the rook is already home to use the file the moment it opens.
moves.teaches: Castle early so your rook is ready to seize the file the instant the centre opens.
moves.plans: Use the open e-file against the stuck king.

moves.spoken: Now the objective crystallises: keep Black's king in the centre. It's hard to shoot a moving target — if the king reaches the kingside the attack restarts from zero. The rook to e1 pins the bishop the moment it appears, chaining the king to its defence.
moves.teaches: Against a stuck king, prevent castling and pin its would-be defenders to keep it exposed.
moves.plans: Re1, pile on the pin, keep the king central.

moves.spoken: First the bishop checks from b5, sidestepping a trade headache — and this light-squared bishop is worth keeping, because Black's pawn to b6 punched holes all over the light squares that only this piece can occupy.
moves.teaches: Preserve the bishop that patrols the colour complex your opponent has weakened.
moves.plans: Keep the light bishop, target the light-square holes.

moves.spoken: After the trade on d7 the queen recaptures, and here's the second flaw: the knight sitting on b4 is loose. The open e-file was never the whole story — a stranded minor piece plus an exposed king is the raw material for a fork.
moves.teaches: Scan for two weaknesses at once — an open line and a loose piece combine into a decisive tactic.
moves.plans: Kick the knight, then fork it with the king.

moves.spoken: The pawn to a3 shoves the knight, and you want to do this regardless of the follow-up: a minor piece parked on your side of the board is a target for pawns. It has to trudge back to a6, and now it's really out of play.
moves.teaches: Push away an intruding minor piece with a pawn — offside knights are pawn-fodder.
moves.plans: a3 to sideline the knight onto a6.

moves.spoken: There it is — the queen to e2 with check. Forget the e-file for a second: this checks the king and, on the same move, rakes the a6-knight down the diagonal. Loose pieces drop off — an exposed king plus an undefended piece is a ready-made fork, and White wins the knight and the game.
moves.teaches: Loose piece + open king = fork; one move that checks and attacks the stray piece wins it.
moves.plans: Qe2+, then capture the loose knight.

moves.spoken: Watch the flexibility: the plan began as stopping Black from castling, and while working on that, two observations — the pressure down the e-file and the vulnerable knight on b4 — merged into the fork. A piece up, the cleanest conversion is to keep trading.
moves.teaches: Let separate observations combine; then, a piece up, simplify to make the advantage tell.
moves.plans: Trade pieces and convert the extra piece.
